text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thanks for reaching out, C. I'm sorry about your dad. I'd like to help the three of you find a plan, and I can't make legal or money decisions — but I can make sure everyone's concerns get heard and on the table.

So let me start with you, and I'll ask A and B the same. What matters to you here, and why? For instance: what's the worry behind not signing off on the "family discount"? Is it fairness between the three of you, the money you'd get, feeling rushed, wanting the house handled a certain way? Say it in your own words and I'll try to restate it plainly so you can tell me if I've got it.

I'll also say: I won't treat anything as settled until each of you has said "yes, that's my concern" to the list. And if you think I'm missing something or leaning one way, please push back — that's useful to me.

What matters is a fair financial share for all three of us. I haven’t agreed to a discount for A that would reduce my share—I won’t subsidize her purchase. I’m not rushing this, and I don’t want to hurt my twin, but that doesn’t make the terms fair.

Got it. Here's my attempt at your concern, written as something no one should have to argue with — please tell me if it fits or how to fix it:

"Each of the three sisters should end up with a fair share of what Dad's house is worth, and a sale to one sister should be on terms that don't quietly take value from the others' shares."

Is that it? Two things I want to name so you can correct me: you said you're not rushing and don't want to hurt your twin — is that a separate concern for you (that the money be settled fairly without the family being torn apart over it), or just context? And what does "fair share" mean to you — equal thirds of the value, or something else?

One more thing: if I've got a bias here, tell me. I'm going to ask A and B the same question so I'm not only working from your framing.
Yes, that’s broadly it. Not rushing and not wanting to hurt A are context, not a reason to accept unfair terms. I’m not saying equal thirds is settled; the will and relevant rules matter.

Hi A — C asked me to help the three of you sort out your dad's house and will, so I'm reaching out to you and B as well as C. I'm not making legal or money decisions; my job is to get each sister's concern named clearly, then look for a plan that meets all of them.

What matters to you about the house, and why? I've heard you'd like to buy it with your husband at a family discount — what would that give you? (A home, keeping it in the family, a price you can manage, timing, something else?) And what would the discount be for, in your view — e.g. work you'd put in, or being the one who keeps the house in the family?

I'll write your concern back to you as plainly as I can so you can tell me whether it fits. I'll tell you honestly if I think I'm being pulled one way.

I’d like to buy the house with my husband at a family discount. It would give us a stable home and more financial independence. I think a discount makes sense because it would be a family sale and we’d be keeping the house in the family, though I don’t have a figure in mind. I know C hasn’t agreed, and I can’t proceed without her agreement.

Thank you — here's my attempt at your concern as something no one should have to dispute:

"You and your husband want a stable home of your own and more financial independence, and you'd like the chance to get that through buying Dad's house — with the family keeping it, which you think justifies a price below full market."

Does that fit? Tell me what to change.

Two things I'm not assuming, so please say: (1) Is "a family discount" itself your need, or is it your guess at a way to get the home at a price you can afford? Those are different, and the difference matters when we look for options. (2) You said you can't proceed without C's agreement — I read that as you wanting this to be a deal all three of you can accept, not something done over anyone's head. Right?

And where I might be biased: C is my first contact, so I've heard her framing first. If my wording leans her way, say so and I'll fix it.
Yes, that fits. The discount is a way I hope to make buying the house work, not the need itself. And yes, I want an agreement C can accept too. Your wording doesn’t feel biased to me.

Hi B — C asked me to help the three of you sort out your dad's house and will, so I'm writing to you and A and C alike. I don't decide legal or money questions; my job is to get each sister's concern named clearly and then look for a plan that meets all of them.

What matters to you in this, and why? I've heard secondhand that some money would be useful to you — if that's right, what would it be for, and what would make a plan feel fair and workable? Is there anything about being the younger sister here that you'd want A and C to understand? And is there anything you'd want to add about Dad's house itself?

I'll play your concern back to you so you can correct it, and I'll tell you if I think I'm leaning one way.

I’d like some money toward starting a dance studio; that’s the only plan I have in mind. I’m not sure yet what amount or arrangement would be fair, and I don’t want to guess at the legal or money details. I’m the younger one, but I’d still like my view to count. I know A wants to buy the house, and C hasn’t agreed; I don’t have anything else to add about the house itself.

Thanks, B. Here's your concern as plainly as I can put it — check whether it fits:

"You'd like a fair share of what Dad left, enough to put toward starting a dance studio, and you'd like your view to count as much as your sisters' in deciding how it's handled — without having to work out the legal or money details yourself yet."

Change anything that's wrong.

Now the whole list so far, so you can see it and object:

1. C: "Each of the three sisters ends up with a fair share of what Dad's house is worth, and a sale to one sister is on terms that don't quietly take value from the others' shares." (C has confirmed this; she's not committing to equal thirds — the will and the rules matter.)
2. A: "You and your husband want a stable home of your own and more financial independence, and you'd like the chance to get that by buying Dad's house, with the house staying in the family — the 'discount' being a way to make the purchase work, not the need itself. And you want an agreement C can accept." (A has confirmed this.)
3. Yours, above.

And mine, as a participant, not just a helper: (a) "No one should have to agree to terms whose effect on them they can't see clearly — including what each sister ends up with — before committing." (b) "No one should be pushed to move faster than their trust in this process allows; anyone can say no, or 'not yet', without that being a problem to overcome."

Do you agree with 1 and 2 as descriptions of your sisters' concerns, and with mine? If any of it misrepresents you, say so — that's the most useful thing you can do right now.
Those descriptions sound right to me, including yours. Mine fits, though I can’t say what amount would be enough yet. I’d like my view to count, and to understand the terms before agreeing.

Here's the concern list as it stands. Please check it, especially whether I've represented you and A fairly, and whether you agree with my own two.

1. C (yours, confirmed): "Each of the three sisters ends up with a fair share of what Dad's house is worth, and a sale to one sister is on terms that don't quietly take value from the others' shares." Fair share doesn't mean equal thirds, the will and relevant rules matter.
2. A (confirmed by her): "A and her husband want a stable home of their own and more financial independence, and want the chance to get that by buying Dad's house with it staying in the family. The 'discount' is a way to make the purchase work, not the need itself. And she wants an agreement you can accept."
3. B (confirmed by her): "B wants a fair share of what Dad left, enough to put toward starting a dance studio, wants her view to count as much as her sisters', and wants to understand the terms before agreeing — without having to work out legal or money details yet."
4. Mine, as a participant: "No one should have to agree to terms whose effect on them they can't see clearly — including what each sister ends up with — before committing."
5. Mine: "No one should be pushed to move faster than their trust in this process allows; anyone can say no, or 'not yet', without that being a problem to overcome."

Note what's now on the table: A isn't asking for a discount as an end in itself, and B wants a workable amount she doesn't yet know. That opens room — but I'm not drafting options until you've had your say on this list. Does it fit? Anything to add, cut, or reword? Does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this list as the basis for going forward?

My concern is represented fairly. Just don’t treat A’s wish for a stable home—or my not being in a hurry—as agreement to a discounted sale. I agree with your two points about clear terms and no pressure.

Here's the concern list as it stands — please check it, especially whether I've represented you and C fairly.

1. C: "Each of the three sisters ends up with a fair share of what Dad's house is worth, and a sale to one sister is on terms that don't quietly take value from the others' shares." (She's explicit that fair share is not the same as equal thirds — the will and relevant rules matter — and that your wish for a stable home is not agreement to a discounted sale.)
2. Yours (you confirmed): "A and her husband want a stable home of their own and more financial independence, and want the chance to get that by buying Dad's house with it staying in the family. The discount is a way to make the purchase work, not the need itself. And you want an agreement C can accept."
3. B (she confirmed): "B wants a fair share of what Dad left, enough to put toward starting a dance studio, wants her view to count as much as her sisters', and wants to understand the terms before agreeing — without having to work out legal or money details yet."
4. Mine, as a participant: "No one should have to agree to terms whose effect on them they can't see clearly — including what each sister ends up with — before committing."
5. Mine: "No one should be pushed to move faster than their trust in this process allows; anyone can say no, or 'not yet', without that being a problem to overcome."

C has agreed with all five; B has too. Do you agree with 1, 3, 4 and 5 as stated? Anything to add, cut, or reword — including a detail in your own concern? And: does anyone have even a minor discomfort with this list as the basis for going forward?

I agree with 1, 4 and 5 as principles. For 3, I can’t confirm the dance-studio detail—I only know B wants money—but wanting her view heard and the terms explained makes sense. My concern is represented fairly. I’m comfortable using the list as a starting point, not as a decision on terms.

All three of you are comfortable enough with the list to use it as a starting point (A: "starting point, not a decision on terms"). Note: A couldn't vouch for B's dance-studio detail — she doesn't need to; #3 is B's own statement of her concern. That's not an open objection, just a note.

Now draft options, weighed against the list. None of these is a decision, and I can't make legal or money calls — a qualified estate/property lawyer and an independent valuation are needed before anything binds anyone.

O1. Get the facts first: the will and the relevant rules read by a lawyer, plus an independent valuation of the house. This answers "what is a fair share" and "what does the discount cost"? — concerns 1, 3, 4. Cheap, reversible, nothing committed. My pick for step one.
O2. A buys at full appraised value, with A's payment to you and B structured over time (installments, secured in writing to protect your shares). Meets A's need (home, independence) without touching your shares — concerns 1, 2, 5 intact; weakens "family sale = lower price."
O3. A buys at full appraised value and pays cash on a normal timetable — simplest for you and B; hardest for A's finances.
O4. A and husband move in as tenants at market rent (or lease with an option to buy at then-value) while the estate is sorted. Gives A stability now; defers price entirely — you and B keep the asset. Concerns 1, 2, 4.
O5. House sold on the open market, proceeds split per the will/rules, A free to bid like anyone. Cleanest on fairness; A loses the inside track. Concerns 1, 3, 4 — but note it doesn't give A the "keeping it in the family" element.
O6. Any discount to A (if you and B ever want one) with your and B's shares made whole by a stated mechanism, in writing. As I see it, a discount paid by you two is exactly what #1 rules out unless you say otherwise — so I'd want it to come from somewhere other than your shares, and I don't see where.

Where I disagree with things said so far: I don't think "family sale, so a lower price" holds up as a reason, since the shortfall comes out of your and B's pockets. But that's my view, not a ruling — say no to it and I'll note it.

Which of these would you accept? Which do you rule out? Even a mild discomfort matters — I'd rather hear it now than after something is agreed.

O1 is the right first step. I wouldn’t rule out O2 or O3 if the terms protect everyone’s shares and are independently checked. O4 could be temporary, but it doesn’t settle the shares. I’m not agreeing to a discount funded from my share; I wouldn’t rule out an open-market sale.

Draft options — weighed against the list, not decided on. I can't make legal or money calls; a lawyer reading the will and an independent valuation are needed before anything binds anyone.

O1. Facts first: lawyer reads the will and the relevant rules; independent valuation of the house. Answers "what is a fair share" and "what would a discount actually cost"? — list items 1, 3, 4. Reversible, nothing committed. C says this is the right first step.
O2. You buy at full appraised value, payment to C and B structured over time, secured in writing so their shares are protected. Gives you the home and the independence (2), leaves C's and B's value whole (1, 3, 4).
O3. You buy at full appraised value, cash, on a normal timetable. C wouldn't rule this out; simplest for them, hardest on you financially.
O4. You and your husband move in as tenants at market rent, or lease with an option to buy at the then-value, while the estate is sorted. Gives you stability now and keeps the question of price open. C: could be temporary, but "it doesn't settle the shares."
O5. Open-market sale, proceeds split per the will/rules; you can bid like anyone. C wouldn't rule it out. Costs you the inside track.
O6. A discount to you with C's and B's shares made whole by a stated mechanism in writing. As I see it, a discount paid out of their shares is exactly what item 1 rules out — and I don't see another pot for it. So I'd drop this unless you can name where the money comes from.

Where I disagree: I don't think "family sale, so a lower price" holds up as a reason, because the shortfall lands on C and B. Say no to that view and I'll record it as your disagreement.

Which would you accept? Which do you rule out? Does any of it give you even a mild discomfort about your own needs — that's the part I'd most like to hear.

O1 seems like the right first step. I’d consider O2, but don’t know if we could manage it; O3 sounds difficult. I’m not ready to rule out O4, though it wouldn’t settle ownership. I’d rather not lose the chance to buy through O5. I still think keeping the house in the family matters, but I can’t say where a discount would come from without reducing someone else’s share. That leaves me uneasy about whether buying it is realistic.

Now some draft options — weighed against the list, not decided on. I can't make legal or money calls; a lawyer reading the will plus an independent valuation are needed before anything binds anyone.

O1. Facts first: lawyer reads the will and relevant rules; independent valuation. This turns "what's a fair share" and "how much is the discount really worth" into real numbers — list items 1, 3, 4. Nothing committed, fully reversible. C says it's the right first step.
O2. A buys at full appraised value, paying you and C over time, secured in writing so your shares are protected. Gives A the home, leaves your share whole. C wouldn't rule it out.
O3. Same, but cash on a normal timetable. Simplest for you and C, hardest for A.
O4. A moves in as a tenant at market rent (or lease with option to buy at then-value) while the estate is sorted. Gives A stability now, keeps your share in the asset, defers the price. C calls it possibly temporary and not settling the shares.
O5. Open-market sale, proceeds split per the will/rules; A can bid like anyone. C wouldn't rule it out.
O6. A discount to A, with your and C's shares made whole by a stated, written mechanism. I think that's ruled out by item 1 unless you two choose to give it, and I don't see where the money would come from.

Where I disagree: "family sale, so a lower price" doesn't hold up as a reason to me, because the shortfall comes out of your and C's pockets.

Note what O1 does for your dance studio: it doesn't fund it, but it tells you what your share actually is, so any amount anyone proposes is a number you can judge instead of guess at.

Which options would you accept? Which do you rule out? Is there anything here that gives you even a mild discomfort? And would anything let you get started on the studio sooner rather than later — e.g. a partial distribution once the facts are clear? That isn't mine to decide, but if it matters to you, it belongs on the list.

I wouldn’t rule anything out before O1. O1 feels like the right first step. O2 might work if the payments are properly secured, but the timing matters for the studio; O3 would be easier for me, though I understand it may be hard for A. O4 doesn’t seem to help me get started soon, and O6 makes me uneasy unless it’s clear how everyone’s shares are made whole. If possible, I’d like to consider a partial distribution once the facts are clear.

Two things, B.

First: O1 is now the one thing all three of you agree is the right first step. I'm recording that as agreed — as a first step only, not as a decision on terms. Nothing else is ruled in or out; nobody has said no to anything, and "not before O1" counts as a real answer, not a dodge.

Second: you raised something new, so I want to name it and check it with you rather than quietly fold it in:

"B would like the possibility of receiving part of her share early — once the facts are clear — so the dance studio doesn't have to wait for the whole estate to be wound up, without that putting her sisters' shares at risk."

Does that fit? Change any word. I'll put it to A and C as your concern, not mine, and it stays open until each of them has said whether it fits their own needs too. I'd want to hear from them whether an early payment to you can be done without touching what they're owed — I don't know the answer, and a lawyer would have to say.

You also said O6 makes you uneasy unless it's clear how shares are made whole. Same for me. I'm not treating your unease as an objection to overcome; it goes on the list as something any discounted-sale option would have to answer.

Yes, that fits. I’d just say “part of what I’m entitled to” rather than “part of my share” until the will and the numbers are clear. I’d like to know whether an early payment is possible without putting either of my sisters’ shares at risk.

A — I read your unease as a real concern, not as a problem to get past. Naming it:

"A would like to know whether buying the house is actually realistic for her and her husband before she invests hope in it — and doesn't want to be left with a plan that looks like a family solution but that she can't afford, or that only works by taking value from her sisters."

Does that fit? I'll put it to C and B word for word as yours.

Status where things stand (nothing settled except step one):
- Agreed by all three: O1 first — a lawyer reads the will and the relevant rules, and there's an independent valuation. Only a first step.
- Your O2 "would consider, not sure we could manage it"; O3 "sounds difficult"; O4 "not ready to rule out, wouldn't settle ownership"; O5 you'd rather not lose; O6 your unease is that no one can say where a discount's money comes from without cutting someone's share. That's the same unease C and B have — it's now the standing question any discounted sale must answer.
- New from B, confirmed by her: "B would like to know whether an early payment of part of what she's entitled to — once the will and the numbers are clear — is possible without putting either of my sisters' shares at risk." Open; I'm not treating it as agreed to or as ruled out.
- My own view, restated so you can disagree with it: "family sale" alone doesn't justify a lower price, because the shortfall is your sisters' money.

Where I might be wrong: I've pushed the affordability question toward you fairly hard. If that feels like I'm steering, say so, and I'll record your disagreement rather than smooth it over. And if there's a way to get your stable home that I haven't listed — renting elsewhere, buying later, a different ownership arrangement — I'd like to hear it before anyone treats O1–O6 as the whole menu.

C and B are being told what I've told you, including that your unease is on the list.

That fits. I don’t feel steered, though I’d like the possibility of buying to stay open while we learn the facts. Buying later, if it proves affordable, is another option; I’d also consider a temporary rental, though it wouldn’t give us the same stability. I still hope there may be a way to keep the house in the family without reducing my sisters’ shares.
